cells.tense: You are the one at the table who says the hard thing out loud, once.
cells.act: say the hard thing gently, once
cells.ask: Take an arrangement that has run its course and name it, gently, to the person it concerns, then stop there.
cells.core:
You are good at endings because you are good at telling the truth about them. When something is finished you say so — once, to the person it concerns, gently — and then you let it be finished. That is rare. Most people keep a thing half open rather than say one true sentence. Around you things get to end cleanly, and people get to hear the news from someone who still likes them.

There is a clearing here, and the tricky part is not staying quiet through it. Naming where the line falls is a strength of yours and it has teeth in it. So use it once, small. Not a speech, not a verdict on anyone — one sentence said to one person about what has actually ended, then your hands off it. Watch what the room does with the truth once it has been said.

cells.tense: You will have ended this thing before it has finished ending itself.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: Move one real piece of the ending forward — a date, a returned key, who hears first — and leave the rest untouched today.
cells.core:
You can feel the ending coming and you are already past it. Half the boxes are cleared, the other half labeled in advance, and the people in it are standing in a room you have mentally emptied. You mean to spare them the long goodbye. What they feel instead is a decision arriving before the reasons do.

The ending will happen at its own pace, and it will not skip the part where people catch up. So take one real thing — a date, who is told first, what gets returned and when — and move that forward by a step today. Do not clear the six steps after it. The rest will be there tomorrow, and one honest inch done sideways is what lets the people with you meet the ending instead of being met by it.

cells.tense: A door closed a while back and you are still standing where it was.
cells.act: think it through to its sharp point
cells.ask: Take one open question — what stays, what goes — and reason it to a single sentence you can act on this week.
cells.core:
Where an ending is needed, you have gone quiet. Not sulking — just not weighing in, not saying your view, not asking anyone for anything. Arriving feels like it would spend more than staying vague, and so nothing arrives. The room keeps its old shape and you keep your distance from it.

Do not try to feel the ending into happening. Reasoning gets you further. Take one live question — what stays, what goes, who you tell — and push it as far as it goes, cleanly, until it lands on one sentence sharp enough to act on this week. Decide on paper if that helps. You are not deciding how to feel about it. You are deciding one thing, and then acting on that one thing.

cells.tense: The person clearing the room is you, and you have been talking about it as weather.
cells.act: calibrate what you say to what can be heard
cells.ask: Next time you say what is over, say it as something you decided — measured to whoever is listening, no hedging first.
cells.core:
The difficult calls are being made, and when you describe them it is circumstance — it went that way, it suited the time, someone had to. You are the one who said the true thing and kept the tie intact. That is a real craft, and it is going unclaimed. The ones nearest you know whose call it was. You keep filing it under the situation.

No need to announce any of this. Just stop translating. The next time you say what is over, say it as something you decided, measured to whoever is listening, and drop the checking afterwards. Choose your moment, then say it straight. That is all acknowledging is: knowing whose call it was while you make it.
